transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-04 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Rao (Zenotech), Carlos Mendes (Zenotech SRE), Aisha Khan (Zenotech ML Eng)

Topics: quantization (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), runtime perf, KV cache, batching, VPC/on-prem benchmarks, accuracy regressions

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We're really excited to walk through the quantization technical review. Liam will drive the SE part, I'll jump in on contractual/pricing bits at the end.

[00:14] Liam Chen: Hey folks, yeah thanks. Quick agenda: talk through quantization options and tradeoffs, show some perf numbers from our lab, dig into KV cache and batching effects, then discuss what we need to run a benchmark in your env. Feel free to interrupt.

[00:30] Dr. Priya Rao: Sounds good. For context, we're running a 7B encoder-decoder variant, mostly generation for RAG and customer support summarization. Latency target is sub-200ms for short prompts, throughput ~200 qps during peak. We're sensitive to hallucinations so accuracy regressions are a big concern.

[00:55] Liam Chen: Great context. So high-level: INT8 gives best perf on many GPUs with quantization-aware kernels but sometimes bigger quality drops on certain layers; FP8 is newer, better for certain fp-native hardware but less broadly supported; GPTQ (post-training quant) is model-specific and can preserve quality but is slower to generate and has some KV cache incompatibilities in our older runtime; AWQ is a newer method that often hits a good perf/quality sweet spot for decoder-only models.

[01:30] Aisha Khan: Quick Q: our stack is on-prem with a VPC-like network and we have HSM for keys. How invasive are the runtime changes for AWQ/GPTQ? We want minimal infra churn.

[01:40] Liam Chen: Good question. For Redwood Private on your VPC, we can run the inference runtime as a managed container set. AWQ/GPTQ are model artifact formats — GPTQ requires an extra preprocessing artifact (quantized weights plus per-tensor scale metadata). Runtime-wise, our newer runtime supports AWQ natively. For GPTQ there's a small compatibility layer; previously it impacted KV cache indexing because of reorderings, but we've added patches to maintain KV cache correctness — though we still recommend re-benchmarking your prompt patterns.

[02:10] Carlos Mendes: When you say KV cache incompatibilities, can you elaborate? Our SRE is worried about long-context statefulness across sessions.

[02:20] Liam Chen: Sure. So KV cache depends on deterministic layer ordering and quantization mapping. Some GPTQ tools reorder weight blocks to pack quantized values which changes the memory layout; that in turn required changes in our KV cache addressing to avoid misalignment. In practice the result is either a small perf hit (extra conversion step on first request) or, if not handled, incorrect tokens beyond the cache boundary. Our latest runtime does a one-time layout conversion at model load for GPTQ artifacts which adds ~150-300ms to load time depending on model size, but runtime decode performance is comparable after that.

[03:00] Dr. Priya Rao: That load time is not ideal for our use-case where we spin up workers on demand, but acceptable for long-lived pools.

[03:12] Liam Chen: Exactly, for short-lived pods INT8 fp16 approaches with faster startup are better. AWQ tends to have smaller load overhead.

[03:30] Maya Patel: Another note: if you do Dedicated reserved capacity that's where the startup time is amortized better. But we'll let Liam handle the deep numbers.

[03:40] Liam Chen: I'll pull up some numbers we collected on A100 and H100 families — keep in mind these are lab numbers and will vary with your CPU/NUMA layout and PCIe topology.

[03:55] Liam Chen: Example 7B decoder-only model: FP16 baseline token p95 latency: 45ms with batch size 1, tokens/sec ~220. INT8 (QK + activation quant) reduced latency to 30ms and increased throughput to ~300 tps. GPTQ (8-bit post-train) produced similar throughput to INT8 but saw a 1.5-2% ROUGE drop on our summarization eval set; AWQ showed only ~0.5% delta but similar throughput gains to INT8.

[04:35] Aisha Khan: 1.5-2% ROUGE drop is concerning. How reproducible is that? And is it data-dependent?

[04:45] Liam Chen: It's model and data dependent. On some models GPTQ is almost lossless, on others it hits certain rare tokens where quant error accumulates. We recommend a small eval prompt set — 200-500 examples — representative of your workloads. That's why the benchmark we asked for in the doc is important.

[05:05] Dr. Priya Rao: Makes sense. We can produce a 500-prompt set focused on our L1-L3 support flows.

[05:15] Carlos Mendes: How does batching interact with KV cache and latency? Our load pattern has many short sessions with single-turn queries.

[05:25] Liam Chen: Batching helps throughput but increases p95 latency for single-turn queries. KV cache reduces tokens generated per request if users are doing multi-turn; it doesn't help single-shot significantly. For bursty short requests we suggest adaptive batching: small dynamic batch window (5-20ms) so you get some batching without exploding tail latency. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with backpressure and latency SLO controls.

[05:55] Dr. Priya Rao: Is continuous batching available in Private? We have network egress restrictions.

[06:03] Liam Chen: Yes, in Redwood Private and Dedicated. It's runtime-level behavior, so as long as the container/pod can run the Redwood agent and has the batching config, it's available. The only caveat is when you use strict air-gapped on-prem we need to ship the agent as an approved image and can work with your security/processes.

[06:25] Aisha Khan: On the topic of FP8: you said it's hardware-dependent. We have a mix of older V100s and a few H100-ish machines. How should we think about FP8 adoption?

[06:37] Liam Chen: FP8 shines on H100s and certain Ampere gen A100 variants with full support in vendor libraries. On V100 you won't get FP8 kernel acceleration so it's not recommended. Practically: if you can move to H100, FP8 gives both perf and energy efficiency wins without the same accuracy risk as naive INT8. But ecosystem and model support is still catching up.

[07:05] Carlos Mendes: Does Redwood's runtime auto-select kernels based on the GPU capability?

[07:10] Liam Chen: Yes, we dynamically pick kernels at model load time based on detected device capability and model shape. We also have a fallback path that uses a scalar-friendly kernel that is slower but compatibile. You can force a kernel policy in the model config if you want reproducible perf across heterogeneous fleets.

[07:30] Maya Patel: Quick interlude: we're going to share a quantization playbook PDF and an AWQ vs GPTQ performance spreadsheet after the call. Liam, you'll attach the sample scripts too?

[07:40] Liam Chen: Yep, I'll drop a benchmark harness script and instructions to run it in Private or Dedicated environments. It includes model load, warmup, perf, and eval phases.

[07:52] Dr. Priya Rao: For security: we need clarity on where the quantized artifacts live and who can download them. Our policy restricts model artifacts to internal S3 and HSM keys for signing.

[08:05] Liam Chen: Under Redwood Private we respect your storage. Model artifacts can remain on your S3; Redwood runtime loads from your bucket via IAM role. We also support signed artifacts and checksum validation. For Dedicated/Hosted the model artifacts live in our storage but we can set up encryption and tenant isolation; however for on-prem you keep everything.

[08:30] Aisha Khan: If we run GPTQ quantization, does Redwood perform the quant conversion or do we need to send GPTQ artifacts?

[08:40] Liam Chen: We can do both. For privacy/regulatory reasons many customers prefer to run GPTQ locally and provide the quantized artifact. We also offer an optional model-onboarding service where Redwood runs GPTQ/AWQ and returns the artifact; in that case we'd operate under an MSA and data handling agreement.

[09:00] Carlos Mendes: Curious about inference memory footprint: approx memory reduction for 7B when moving to INT8 vs FP16?

[09:10] Liam Chen: Roughly ~2x memory reduction when moving FP16->INT8 ignoring optimizer states. So a 7B model that uses ~16GB in FP16 might drop to ~8-9GB in INT8. AWQ/GPTQ numbers are similar but depend on extra scale tables. Also note KV cache memory is still proportional to sequence length and hidden size, so you'll still need memory headroom for long contexts.

[09:40] Dr. Priya Rao: Right. Our top concern besides accuracy is deterministic decoding across restarts — we need identical outputs for certain compliance checks. Do quantized models introduce non-determinism?

[09:55] Liam Chen: Quantization per se is deterministic if you use fixed scaling and deterministic kernels. Issues arise with mixed-precision kernels that utilize non-deterministic fused ops or async GPU operations. We have a deterministic build flag that forces reproducible kernels at the cost of some perf; it's available in Redwood Private builds.

[10:20] Maya Patel: Great note. We'll flag that in the doc.

[10:28] Aisha Khan: Regarding eval metrics: you mentioned ROUGE earlier. Do you have examples of prompts that are most affected by GPTQ?

[10:36] Liam Chen: Yes, we saw issues on long-question-answer pairs with rare entities and on structured generation (tables/JSON) where small probability shifts matter. We'll include example prompts in the dataset we share.

[10:52] Dr. Priya Rao: Operational question: when you say model load conversion for GPTQ, is that a disk I/O bound op or GPU bound? We need to budget for load concurrency.

[11:02] Liam Chen: Mostly CPU + memory copy bound to reorganize tensors on host before sending to GPU. It can be parallelized but still eats host CPU during load. If you're doing high churn we recommend a small pool of warmed workers or pre-converted images.

[11:25] Carlos Mendes: Can we cache converted artifacts so subsequent startups are fast?

[11:30] Liam Chen: Absolutely, we support caching the converted model layout on disk — a conversion cache key based on model hash. That eliminates repeated conversions.

[11:40] Aisha Khan: On the topic of benchmarks: what metrics should we provide back to you to make a decision? Latency p50/p95, tokens/sec, and ROUGE is okay? Anything else?

[11:50] Liam Chen: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec), memory footprint, GPU utilization, and a small accuracy table (ROUGE/BLEU or accuracy for classification) plus sample diffs on failing prompts. Also, model load time and cache warmup time.

[12:10] Dr. Priya Rao: Ok we'll run those.

[12:18] Maya Patel: Quick reminder — pricing/packaging will vary if you go Dedicated vs Private. We'll outline the options in the follow-up email.

[12:30] Liam Chen: One more nuance: AWQ is particularly nice for decoder-only; for encoder-decoder models (like your base) AWQ support has improved but we recommend extra eval because cross-attention layers sometimes behave differently under some quant rules.

[12:50] Aisha Khan: We're 80% decoder-only use for the customer-facing agent, but our internal summarizer is encoder-decoder, good to know.

[13:02] Carlos Mendes: Any gotchas with SSO and RBAC when running Private? We need to map roles to teams and restrict model download.

[13:12] Liam Chen: Redwood Private supports SAML/SSO, LDAP, and fine-grained RBAC. Model artifact permissions can be enforced via IAM roles in your bucket. We'll include an architecture note in the security doc.

[13:30] Dr. Priya Rao: If we see a 1-2% quality regression on GPTQ, how do we decide whether to accept? Is there a way to do hybrid routing (some traffic to FP16 fallbacks)?

[13:45] Liam Chen: Yes, you can do model routing: e.g., serve 90% queries to quantized model and 10% to FP16 for higher-quality responses or route specific prompt classes to FP16. Redwood supports A/B rollouts and automatic fallback policies on quality regressions detected by your eval harness.

[14:05] Maya Patel: That is one of the things Redwood Console's Rollouts feature handles — you can configure canary percents and auto-fallback.

[14:15] Aisha Khan: Are there any security concerns with transferring quantization metadata? Like scale tables revealing something about the model?

[14:25] Liam Chen: Not really; scale tables are numeric transforms and don't leak training data. The bigger concern is the model weights themselves. Still, we treat all artifacts as confidential. We can also sign and encrypt artifacts if required.

[14:40] Carlos Mendes: Ok. For the benchmarking step, can Redwood run an agent in our VPC and pull metrics? Or will we have to push logs to Redwood?

[14:50] Liam Chen: Both options supported. For strict networks we provide an offline harness that writes artifacts to an S3 you control; alternatively we can run a short-lived agent in your VPC that pushes aggregated metrics to Redwood telemetry bucket.

[15:05] Dr. Priya Rao: Let's do offline for now, we prefer to keep telemetry internal.

[15:12] Maya Patel: Sounds good. To confirm next steps: Liam will send the AWQ/GPTQ spreadsheet, benchmark harness and playbook; Zenotech will assemble a 500-prompt eval set, whitelist our runner IPs or use offline mode, run the harness, and share results. We'll meet the week of 2026-03-09 to review.

[15:32] Dr. Priya Rao: Yep that's correct. Also we'll provide a list of target p95 and allowed quality delta for decisioning.

[15:40] Carlos Mendes: I'll open the firewall ticket today and add the team.

[15:45] Aisha Khan: Any final notes on long-term operational costs? Does INT8 always save costs?

[15:53] Liam Chen: Generally yes — INT8 and AWQ reduce GPU memory and peak utilization, which lowers effective cost. But if you have to route a percentage to FP16 for quality, math changes. We'll help model the unit economics based on your request patterns in the follow-up.

[16:10] Maya Patel: Great. Thank you all for the time. We'll circulate the docs and set the follow-up.

[16:18] Dr. Priya Rao: Thanks everyone.

[16:20] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription; occasional mis-hearings (e.g., "AWQ" sometimes transcribed as "A W Q"; "KV cache" as "K V cache").

Shared artifacts referenced: quantization_playbook.pdf (link in follow-up), awq_vs_gptq_perf.xlsx, benchmark_harness.zip
